title: In 1851 a pendulum in Paris showed Earth spinning without a glance at the sky

cover.alt: Foucault’s pendulum swinging under the dome of the Panthéon in Paris, its brass bob hanging on a long wire above a circular scale on the floor.

body: Léon Foucault hung a 28 kg brass-coated lead bob on a 67 m wire from the dome of the Panthéon and set it swinging. Hour by hour the line of its swing crept clockwise across the floor, about **11.3° an hour** in Paris, a full circle in roughly 32 hours. The pendulum keeps swinging in the same plane; it is the floor, and the whole Earth beneath it, that turns. It was the first simple, direct demonstration of Earth’s rotation that needed no star or Sun to watch.

slides.question: In Paris, how many hours does the swing plane take to come full circle?
slides.explanation: About 32 hours (the article gives 31.8 h). The rate depends on latitude: one day at the pole, slower towards the equator, where it stops altogether.

slides.question: Where would a Foucault pendulum’s swing plane never drift at all?
slides.explanation: On the equator Earth’s spin axis lies flat in the pendulum’s horizon, so there is no rotation about the vertical and the plane stays put. At the poles it turns once a day.

slides.alt: Animation: a side view of Foucault’s pendulum under the Panthéon dome tips into a top view of a brass compass-rose floor dial. In time-lapse the swing line turns clockwise, 11.3° an hour, a full turn in 31.8 hours; then dials at the pole, Paris and the equator compare the rates.

slides.label: an hour: the drift of the swing plane at the latitude of Paris
slides.text: Foucault measured about 2.3 mm of sideways drift at the bob’s edge on every swing of the 16.5-second pendulum.

slides.heading: Hours for the swing plane to turn full circle
slides.note: The pole takes one sidereal day, 23 h 56 min. At the equator the plane never turns

slides.heading: Why latitude matters
slides.text: At the pole the pendulum’s plane stays fixed in space while Earth turns beneath it once a day. Elsewhere only part of Earth’s spin is around the local vertical, so the drift is slower: 360° times the sine of the latitude per day, which comes to zero at the equator.
